title: Metta Sutta, Part 4: The Teachings on Loving Kindness
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett reflects on their experience practicing loving-kindness meditation through the Heart Sutra, highlighting the importance of recognizing and releasing conditional thinking that can lead to unconditioned positive emotions towards ourselves and others. They emphasize the interconnectedness of four paramita practices - metta, mudita, compassion, and equanimity - and the need to cultivate balance and resilience in our emotional responses. By letting go of our own conditioning and limitations, we can awaken to a more authentic and compassionate practice of loving-kindness that sees all beings as whole and worthy of love and support.

sentences.text: Good evening everybody, thanks for being here.
I'm just back a couple of days ago from the Mexican town of San Miguel de Allende, where I went to do a couple of events.
The main part was a three-day study retreat on the Heart Sutra.
All the little chants are translated into Spanish, and we only do them in Spanish, so I've learned a lot of them.
It was like I had to condition myself for a moment or not to say, "Buenas noches, un suberable, inamorable," blah blah blah.
I don't remember that one though, but I remember at the end of the service, *Todos los buddhas otra vez al espacio y al tiempo*.
It's nice, huh?
It was really, really nice to get to go down there.
There aren't so many opportunities to practice, so people get a little more excited and they take the bus for four hours, six hours, ten hours to get there.
It turned out to be a place that people really loved to go in Mexico, so it had the double appeal of going to a favorite place, a beautiful place, and also getting to practice together.
I want to see if we can say a few more words about the Metta Sutra.
I'm trying to finish this little cycle of talks which has sort of popped up like things do and then vanished and popped up again.
It's been a couple of weeks since the last one, but I think they're all on the website; you can listen.
I brought more copies of this comparison of different translations if you don't have one or don't have one handy.
I just want to flag a few of the themes from previous talks.
I'm curious if you've been thinking about these things.
One is that this Sutra, this encouragement to generate loving-kindness, to generate Metta for all beings, like everywhere.
You just chanted this.
You notice that it's like not just like, we don't just mean everywhere; we really mean everywhere: born, unborn, small, big, visible, invisible, all beings.

One of its sort of central qualities is that these wishes—these wishes for happiness, for well-being, for others—are unconditioned wishes, unconditioned wishes that don't have any strings attached, don't have any ideas of strings that could be attached.

One of the things I've been suggesting that we all look at is how often the mind is a little bit conditional, maybe a lot bit conditional: "I will like you if," "I will appreciate what you just did if," "you will receive this gift from me if," "you develop a pattern of acting in a certain way that I like," and so on.
And of course, we do this with ourselves as well: "I will appreciate myself if I have such and so sort of mental states or story or something."

This is an encouragement to notice that conditionality that we're adding, and that it's an addition, and that we can release from that and be unconditionally positive towards ourselves and others, whether it makes sense or not, you know, so-called makes sense.
When did makes sense get to be God, you know?
Makes sense is our God; we have to admit this.
If something happens, it doesn't make sense.
It's like, you know, it's sacrilege and we're upset, you know, our God has been offended.
Something didn't make sense.
I think that's really true.
The other thing which I don't think about it before is that Metta exists usually in a constellation of four practices, but they all have this unconditional quality.
I want to mention the other three because this is really kind of axiomatic of Buddhism.
Whenever one teaching is mentioned, usually there's a lot of other things being referenced.
Usually a whole list of other practices are being referenced.
We were noticing this about the Heart Sutra; it seems to be about wisdom, prajnaparamita, wisdom beyond wisdom.
But then wisdom also, that practice includes five other practices or ten other practices or whatever.
So Metta includes three other practices.
The first is generosity.
You have to be generous, you know, and actually practice being generous to support this wish, this wish for joy and happiness for others.
I'm confusing my list, but anyway, I'll just go on anyway as if I knew what I was talking about.
Another is a really good one for which there's no single English word.
The Pali is mudita, which means feeling joy in the joy of another.
They usually translate this as sympathetic joy.
You have the ability to actually feel something when somebody else feels something; you can actually feel something.
This is possible.
If they're experiencing something positive, you can feel good for them.
And not just, you know, again, like I'm conditioned not just like "good for you," you know, but actually to directly experience like pleasure and joy that somebody else is happy.
A clever German invented a word that means the opposite of that, right?
Do you know that word?
Schadenfreude, taking pleasure in somebody's misery.
So it's the opposite of Schadenfreude.
Then we have, yeah, donna wasn't on this list, but it's still a good practice compared to generosity.
We have Metta, mudita, and we have compassion, which is a close ally of Metta.
So Metta, loving kindness, is the sort of positive side of the equation—the just aspiration and yearning for all beings to be just happy, peaceful, everything to work well.
And then compassion is the suffering side of that equation.
Of course, there's always suffering as well.
So compassion is the ability to feel the suffering of others in a wholesome, positive way that actually would lead to something good happening.
So Metta is the love, and compassion is being able to feel the suffering in a positive, sympathetic way.
The last one, which is kind of like the linchpin, usually the last one on the list, is like the, you know, sort of the linchpin of the thing.
Like wisdom is the linchpin of the paramita practices.
The last one is equanimity, upekkhā, equanimity.
So can we engage in all these like, you know, emotional, dynamic, interpersonal, you know, sort of shared realities?
Love, suffering, joy, sorrow, right?
Can we engage in all that in a way that somehow has got some balance or resilience to it?
I think sometimes we misunderstand equanimity.
You mean like it's sort of cold and unfeeling or something like that, like, you know, not going to feel anything.
But somehow it's the ability to come back to the middle, you know, even if you're only there for a millisecond, you know.
You can come back again, come back again, like the little weebly wobbly toy.
We got as far in three talks.
We got through three sets of verses in this little chart.
Actually, this is a poem in Pali with a very clear verse structure.

The left column has the Pali, the middle column has a very little translation from Thanissaro Bhikkhu, who is a very reliable scholar of early Buddhism, an American guy and a monk, and the right has a wee chant.
We got as far as number four.
After "may all beings be happy," we start to list what kind of beings we mean: weak, strong.
And here the translations agree with each other because it's just a simple list of adjectives: high, middle, low, small, great.
Whether we can see them or not, we chant that.
We don't think about it for a minute.
This is wishing well-being upon beings we can't even see.
Near, far, born or to be born.
May all beings be happy.
I think there are two ways to see such a list.
One way is that they figure we probably didn't get it the first time when they said "all beings"; they want to make sure we really get it, and that's useful.
Our minds are pretty stubborn; it's good, actually.
No, I really mean all beings, without exception.
Another way to look at it is actually its meditation instructions: that you should very deliberately and maybe systematically think about bringing forth loving-kindness towards weak beings.
Really practice that way for like a month or a year.
Really notice beings that seem to you weak or think about beings that seem weak and really wish loving-kindness in them.
Once you have a little facility for that, strong beings.
Beings that may be in your conditional mind, you think, "well, they don't really need my help."
Wealthy and poor should be in here, too; that would be good for us.
So to see it that way, whatever realm of existence they're in, we still wish them happiness and joy.
Well, smaller, great, there's our rich guys.
I was telling a few folks that San Miguel de Allende has quite a strong, a large expatriate American community.
By and large, these are very wealthy people who own large houses and probably one of several houses of their part of the year.
It seems to be that it's a mixed bag in that Mexican town.

On the one hand, it's like a Santa Fe or a Manhattan or something where everything's gentrified and the regular people can't afford to live in the center of the town anymore, although they did pretty well when they sold out.
So the rich people from America have the nice houses, and they are a little bit of a separate society.
Most of them don't speak Spanish very well, if at all.
Actually, some of them speak no Spanish.
I talked to a woman who lived there since 1990, and she had like half a dozen words in her accent; it was atrociously bad, even I could tell.
It has more nonprofit service organizations and charities than any town in the entire country.
So they do hang around in their beautiful houses and do good all day.
The orphanages are well-funded; they're actually like reasonable social services, whereas this is a huge problem in Mexico—apparently there's basically no social services.
But here in this town, you know, the Rotary puts on a gala dinner at the nice restaurant, and voila, you've got health care.
So these are great beings; we can wish them well.
Or are they small-minded beings?
Or both, you know.
So visible and invisible is curious.
Like we think if we can't see it, it doesn't exist.
But in Western science and philosophy, we make a big distinction between the material and the mental.
This distinction is not so true in Buddhist thought.
So visible beings and invisible beings, they're here.
And sometimes we have unusual experiences where it seems like there might be invisible beings; you know, things happen.
Not even beings that haven't been born yet, you know.
So this is really thorough, and we can really practice that way.
Then we enter a new section.
This is verse six.

The very first part had a sort of interesting blend of, on the one hand, a kind of intention to be wise and good, on the other hand, a kind of acknowledgement that this is what happens if you're wise and good.
Then there was an intention about how to act, to wish things for other beings.
Starting in verse six, we enter the realm of relationship because now we're talking about deceit, you know, and despising other beings, and wishing harm and anger.

So this is calling for us to actually look at what our attitude really is, besides just sort of like some kind of, not just sort of kind of an affirmation practice, like "I'm just going to talk myself into loving other beings."
We actually look, "well, how do I really behave in relationship to other beings?
Am I truly honest and straightforward?"
Here we have the precepts, really.
In verse six, this kind of stands for all of the precepts, all the ethical guidelines.
How are we going to live with other beings?
And of course, meditation supports all of this.
Maybe we become a little more self-aware, a little more space in our mind in between impulse and reaction.
Another great virtue of liturgical practice is how great it is that we chant this text.
This is not a traditional Zen text to chant; this has been in the Soto Zen world for maybe fifteen or twenty years only.
And actually, our own guiding teacher, Norman Fischer, was one of the architects of this happening, one of several.
But now it's not unusual to chant the Metta Sutta and send centers all over the West.
I don't know if this has trickled back to Japan, probably not.

If you chant this sometimes, and you chant it a lot, and it gets memorized and in your body in a certain way, sometimes it really helps in that little phrases from these texts just pop into your mind when you need them.
In other words, this is not just a sort of rational, it's not just serving the God of rationality to chant these texts and study these texts.

But sometimes, you know, you're about to fly off the handle, and you're convinced that you're right, and she or she is a complete whatever, you just pop in your mind, "Let none be by anger or hatred."
Whoa, whoops, yes.
So this is what waking up actually means, right?
To wake up to our own conditioning.

It's nice when we're in a good mood and we're with our sangha buddies and we're thinking about these things, but it's really awakening when it comes, when it's needed, when Buddha speaks to us in that way.
Let's look at line seven, verse seven.
This is one of the most famous lines from the sutra.
It uses the metaphor of a mother and her child to see all beings as if they were your children.
The Tibetans are particularly good at thinking this way, and this is a famous teaching from the Tibetan schools.

Part of why you would unconditionally love and appreciate others is if rebirth is a given and endless sort of vast spans of cosmological time are given, then without doubt, everybody you meet at one time or another was your mother.
Every single person.
So you would not treat your mother that way, right?
You'd give your mother the benefit of the doubt, but this is your mother.
"Dave is my mother."
Good question.
Thanks, Mom.
I appreciate it a lot.
This is kind of riffing on that same sensibility to treat other beings as if they were a child in danger and you are their mother.
In Mexico, they had trouble with this line.
The trouble was it's really weird to have only one child; like something's wrong.
That would be a reference to something not being right in the family.
There's only one child.
So they changed it to *niños*, plural, so they would not worry about that and focus on the point of the text.
I get disturbed; I'm like, "well, why does she only have one child?
What happened?
Is she okay?"
I think the whole Mexican families are getting smaller, like families all over the world.
I met people with only two or three children, but I don't know if I ever met anybody there with one child.
So, boundless mind.
I'm not sure what's being translated for boundless.
Thanissaro uses "limitless heart," "limitless heart."
It's a big heart and a big mind.
The next part, verse eight, is again a kind of meditation instruction, which is that this makes sense to our rational mind if we're thinking about individual people whom we know.
I can wish Ken happiness and well-being because I can kind of visualize him.
I think in my mind I know who he is, and he's the person over there and all that.
But this is saying that's not enough.
It needs to be bigger than just people that we know and can make sense of.
We want to send this loving kindness over the whole world, not even just the whole world, above the world, below the world, all around the world, limitlessly.
So it's a cultivation practice.
Here it looks like "cultivate" is true to the original Pali, but we're going to come up, coming soon, to a big difference between the two translations.
This came up at the very beginning, too, so let me kind of refer back to that.
If you go back to verse number one, there's a big difference in attitude here, and I think it's a really useful thing to contemplate.
The more literal translation in the middle column, I'll read it: *This is to be done by one skilled in aims who wants to break through to the state of peace.

Be capable, upright, and straightforward, easy to instruct, and so on.* The first one is saying there's some level of acknowledgement that you have some skill; otherwise, you wouldn't be contemplating this practice.
But you're kind of like on the wrong side of something; you're in a limited being in some way who needs development and improvement.
That through this, you'll break through to peace.
You are not current, so therefore, you're not peaceful.
You are not peaceful.
So there's something wrong with you.
And, you know, right?
Who can argue that?
There's something wrong with us, and here's some medicine, here's some tools to help us.

That's the kind of, in broad strokes, a dominant attitude in early Buddhism: that there's something wrong with us, but this is a very skillful, fantastic system for us to become awakened beings, better beings.
But then the one on the right, which is sort of somewhat of a free translation by American Zen teachers mostly, has more of a sort of later Buddhism feeling.
The later Buddhism feeling is more like, well, the whole problem is that you think there's something wrong with you.
Relax.
You are complete.
You are whole.
You have been gifted with this precious human birth.
You have everything you need.
Even your problems are exactly perfect; they're exactly the right problems for you.
The key here is to stop telling yourself that you're broken and on the wrong side of something and to recognize your inherent goodness.
These are like the Buddha nature teachings, right?
Tathagatagarbha teachings.
The moon of the Buddha is in us.
So our translation therefore says, this is what should be accomplished by the one who is wise.
See, big difference, you know?
A couple words.
Is wise, already wise, and is therefore seeking the good, has obtained peace.
So already has it.
Complete opposite there.
So, they messed with it a little bit here.
Yeah, they did.
But it's good.
What's lucky for us is that we're in a time and place where we have access to both of these kind of major schools of thought, and they're both helpful.
If we just sort of hung around and said, oh, you know, we're fine and we're not going to pay any attention, that's no good.
But if we constantly tell ourselves we're broken, that's no good either.
So there's kind of a holding opposites, right?
To feel into our wholeness and our completeness and our peacefulness.
There's already peacefulness there.
And to be skillful in working with our non-peacefulness.
This is going to show up again here at the very end.
It shows up strongly at the beginning and the ending.
So, verse nine: Standing or walking.
This is like more meditation instruction; this is really good instruction.
We would do well to not sort of just skip over this.
Not to think that everything has to be configured in a certain way for us to be practicing fully as bodhisattvas, as practitioners.
We don't have to be at the zendo.
We don't have to be in a good mood.
Every posture, every time, every place, and not only to practice, but practice with gratitude.
To be grateful that we have this opportunity, even when we're not enjoying the opportunity in life.
To bring out great gratefulness.
It's a little bit different from the literal translation, which does not actually even mention gratitude.
I bet the word gratitude is probably not in the Pali.
I do have a very exhaustive Pali by Pali, word by word thing in Pali; I can send it to you if you want to know.
Then we're into the wisdom piece of this whole text.
The text has roughly sort of three parts.
It has, and this is typical of all Buddhist texts, in some way they're always referring to three things.
They're referring to ethical conduct, how should we act, they call it.
They're referring to compassion in some way.
There's a very positive compassion piece of this.
And then they're referring to wisdom.
The wisdom piece is, how do you really understand the world if you practice thoroughly with this?
And what will be the results of this understanding?
The literal version is again representing back to rebirth.
In early Buddhism, the idea was, not only is there something wrong with you, there's something inherently wrong with this entire conditioned world.
It's just a little messed up or a lot messed up.
And the goal is to basically leave.
We're trying to slow down, right?
So what's the natural result of slowing down, and slowing down, and slowing down, and slowing down?
It's stopping.
The goal of early Buddhism was to stop, to really stop, to get off the wheel, to stop being reborn and just enter something that they call nirvana.
So if you read the literal one here, it says, *not taken with views, but virtuous and consummate in vision, having subdued desire for sensual pleasure, one never again will lie in the womb*.
Whoa, yeah.
Just stay out of wombs.
Kick your womb habit.
Stop being reborn.
This is kind of early Buddhist sensibility.
It sounds a little creepy, too, but there's a beauty to it.
This is a complete peacefulness.
To us, it sounds a little dead, maybe.
So here it gets rewritten as, *not holding to fixed views, that's the same, endowed with insight, freed from sense appetites, pretty much the same*.
One who achieves the way will be freed from the duality of birth and death.
Another angle on birth and death, and freed from duality, again, kind of looking in a very big way at wholeness, that this life is whole and complete, including death, including birth.
There are many metaphors to this.
I was just telling you that the Heart Sutra is all about emptiness.
This is kind of an emptiness teaching, too.
I brought up the usual metaphor of the waves and the ocean.
Do you know this metaphor?
Because of our point of view and our sort of self-referential thinking, we think we're separate.
I'm over here and you're over there, and we have our own trajectory and different things happen, and you're this kind of person I know because of the shape of your face or something.
We have all these judgments and stuff.
We feel like we have this separate little life, and this life that started at about 2:15 a.m. on January 17, 1966, and it's going to end here, knows when, but it could be soon, it could be later.
The metaphor of the wave and the ocean is that because you're just looking from wave top to wave top, you just have this narrow vision.
You're looking through a bamboo tube, that's another metaphor they say, and reality.
You see these little separate people, and what you need to do is look down.
If you look down, you see we're all part of this big ocean.
What happens when another wave disappears into the ocean?
Is it dying?
No.
It's just the ocean expressing itself.
It's just an expression of life.
Life expresses in a certain way.
One wave looks a little different from the other one; it breaks differently and slightly different color, and so on.
That's a little bit of this or that inside the wave, but then it's just the ocean.
That's more or less what they're trying to say here, I think, about being freed from the duality of birth and death and this idea of separation.
What's the biggest separation of all?
Death, which is why we fear it so much.
But the fear is because of point of view.
Fear is because of a strongly held point of view that is so strongly held and so convincing that we can't imagine any other view.
We can use metaphor and meditation and chant this stuff over and over again.
Here's a nice little story.
When I earlier was teaching, this is like somewhat of a repeat, an encore edition or something.
I prepared most of this in 2009, I have to admit.
But we're doing the chant book, so it seemed worth airing.
Back then I was listening to some lectures on this text by Bhikkhu Bodhi, another great American translator of early Buddhism and a monk as well.
Bhikkhu Bodhi and Thanissara Bhikkhu both have written a lot.
I was listening to lectures, I found some lectures online of Bhikkhu Bodhi lecturing about the Metta Sutta.
He told this story that he was staying somewhere and there was a woman there who was a very smart person who said she'd just finished her training to be a lawyer, but she was having this big problem.
Perfectly smart, capable person, but she could not get a job.
The reason why she could not get a job is she was just horrible in job interviews.
She would walk into the room and just become sort of just unable to speak clearly and couldn't think straight, and just looked like the last person in the world you want to hire to be your lawyer.
She was perfectly eloquent other times.
She asked Bhikkhu Bodhi for advice, and he thought of the line about the mother.
He thought of that line from chanting and suddenness that popped into his mind.
He said, "Next time you're in the interview, just put yourself in the place of your mother, wishing love and support and kindness for everybody in the room.
Just shift your point of view, like walk in there like you're the mother.
You're not even the kid, you're the mother."
The woman said, "That's no good for me.
I have a really terrible relationship with my mother."
And maybe that's the whole problem here, actually, now that you mention it.
She had a whole kind of realization in that moment, he says, that her mother was never able to express any love for her, always criticizing her, never said a positive thing.
I was actually talking to a friend whose parent died recently.
What she said was, she realized that she was not mourning her parent; she was mourning that she never got to have the positive relationship with her parent that she always longed for.
So maybe this woman will end up with that, I don't know.
Anyway, that was no good.
These teachings don't always work, right?
The simile of the mother and her child wasn't helpful to that woman.
So Bhikkhu Bodhi took another tack.
He knew this woman really cherished her relationship with her Dharma teacher.
Someone expressed a lot of compassion for her and love for her.
So he suggested that she go into the job interview, imagine yourself to be a teacher interviewing the students.
That the hiring committee are her students, and she can show up with love and compassion.
She went back to the interviews and went much better.
But she didn't actually get the job, he said, because actually it was the wrong specialty in law.
But the interview went really well.
She felt calm and compassionate.
She was able to interact with the other people in the interview by establishing that feeling before she went in of being her own teacher.
She said the interview committee was really impressed and was wishing they had another position to hire her.
Isn't that nice?
These teachings can really shape our attitude in really fundamental ways.
I don't know if you have anything else to say just to see what you have to say about all this.
Sorry to be a little scattershot here.
Oh, here's a definition of rebirth.

According to some encyclopedia somewhere, rebirth in Buddhism is the doctrine that the consciousness of a person upon death or dissolution of the aggregates, the skandhas, becomes one of the contributing causes of the arising of a new group of skandhas, a person, in other words.
The consciousness arising in the new person is neither identical to nor different from the old consciousness.
There's a walk in this line, but forms part of the causal continuum or stream within it.
The basic cause for this persistent re-arising of personality is the abiding of consciousness and ignorance.
Because we're confused, we get reborn all the time.
Then the Bodhisattva teachings of course kind of turn that and say, "I'm going to be deliberately ignorant.
If that's what it takes, I'll be ignorant.
Because I need to go back in there and help people.
Help beings.
Because I'm practicing having loving kindness for all beings as best I can."
What do you think of all that?
If you weren't here, do listen to the other talks.
In my first talk I led a version of the loving kindness practice.
There's actual practice that you do with this.
It's nice to do.
You can do it on your own, but actually it's really nice to have somebody lead you through it.
It's a kind of systematic kind of way of working with different kinds of relationships and bringing up loving kindness.
So what do you think of the Metta Sutta?
Do you always enjoy chanting it?
Do you think it's a little weird?
Be honest.
Yeah, I chant a lot.
It's important because sometimes situations lead to pain and negativity in relationships.
If you are thinking about loving kindness, it's much more likely that you will strive for that, even after whatever has happened.
And then eventually you will clear your own field and be more peaceful.
That's nice.
I think one of the things these teachings would also encourage in the mix there, which is part of what you said, is some real curiosity about the causal links there.
You said a situation happens that leads to negativity.
So it's a great thing to be curious.
Well, how does it lead to that?
Does it always lead to that?
I was thinking about alcoholism.
Alcoholism is a powerful cause.
That in itself is just so endlessly confusing and doesn't really lead to love in my experience, unless the person stops drinking.
Being a spouse or a lover for that just often leads to a lot of pain and stuff in the long run.
May all the people who are caught in the grip of addiction find peace and be happy, find happiness, real happiness.
Any thoughts about the translations or the text?
The line that always catches me emotionally, I'm not sure if I've spent enough time with it to figure out why, but it's the third section.
*Let one do nothing that is mean, or that the wise would be cruel.
May all beings be happy.
May they be joyous and live in safety.* That always catches me.
About the wise?
No, the part about, well, it's the whole thing, but let one do nothing that is mean, or that the wise would be cruel.
Especially I think when you're a kid, you think of things that that person is mean, probably just because they're not doing what you want to do.
But there are situations where one should know better than to mistreat others.
And that's why people do that.
They mistreat others.
When you're really little, maybe you don't know where, I want the tricycle and that's it.
But later on, you have some better understanding.

I always appreciate that the wise may reprove part, because that's such a great yoga for those sort of morally ambiguous moments, where you're doing something where you're kind of telling yourself, "Well, this is okay to do, but I don't really want to tell anybody what I'm doing, but it really is okay."
I say so.
So yeah, that you would be willing, whatever choice you make, to bring it before the wise and ask for their blessing.
And they say, "No, you really got to take that scotch tape back to work, man.
That's stealing."
But we got to practice a little stuff.
We've got about call time.
Anyone want to say anything else?
Just to say that it's accessible.
Of all our sutras, you don't need to develop understanding.
You don't need to develop faith.
You can go right into this.
That's great.
I just spent three days talking nonstop about the Heart Sutra.
What do they mean?
No eyes.
This is great that way.
And it's good we're also going to have texts.
Both, I think, are good.
And kind of the opposite thing, don't you think?
Like, it's great that we also have texts that are confusing and obscure and about light and darkness and kind of messing with our simple ideas about reality.
We all said we need both so that we can kind of go deep and go warm.
Okay.
Thanks very much.
My pleasure.

verbatim.text: Good evening everybody, thanks for being here. So I'm just back a couple days ago from the Mexican town of San Miguel de Allende. I got to go down there and do a couple of events. The main part was a three-day study retreat on the Heart Sutra. So all the little chants are translated into Spanish, and we only do them in Spanish, so I've learned a lot of them.
